headline: Dark mornings, default AI, and 107,000 species for sale
teaser: Who pays for brighter evenings? Should a search engine come bundled with AI? And can we call a trade sustainable if no one counts it?

articles.title: Brighter Evenings, Darker Mornings: The Hidden Cost of Permanent Daylight Saving Time
articles.dek: Ending the clock change sounds like pure convenience. A new study asks who would pay for the extra evening light.
paras: Twice a year, most Americans adjust their clocks: forward an hour in spring and back an hour in autumn. The ritual is widely unpopular, and in July 2026 the US House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act, a bill that would end the autumn change and keep the country on daylight saving time (DST) all year. The bill has since stalled in the Senate, but nineteen states have already approved measures that would take effect if it becomes law. Supporters often present the change as a simple matter of convenience. A new study from the University of Washington, published in Current Biology in late October, suggests that the choice involves a less visible trade-off, one that falls heavily on children.

To understand this trade-off, it helps to remember what a clock change actually does. Shifting the clock does not create additional daylight; it only moves hours of light from one end of the day to the other. Under permanent DST, winter sunsets would come an hour later, giving people brighter evenings for shopping, sport, and outdoor leisure. The price would be paid in the morning. In December and January, when days are already short, sunrise in many places would arrive after 8 a.m., and in communities at the western edge of a time zone, considerably later than that.

The researchers, led by postdoctoral scholar Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante and biologist Horacio de la Iglesia, set out to measure what this would mean for students. Using school start times, enrollment figures, and school locations in 14 states that have voted to adopt permanent DST if Congress allows it, they counted how many trips to school would begin before sunrise under each system. Their analysis led them to estimate that, across the United States, permanent DST would add at least 2 billion dark school commutes every year. Georgia alone would see roughly 71 million additional dark trips, while in Alabama and Mississippi the number would climb from about 2 million to more than 20 million each. Because the team assumed that students leave home at 8 a.m., which is relatively late, the authors describe their figures as conservative.

Why does darkness matter? The first concern is safety. Examining crash records, the team found that fatal accidents involving school-age pedestrians were roughly twice as likely on dark mornings as after sunrise. The researchers are careful to note that this finding does not reveal exactly how many extra crashes permanent DST would cause, since drivers and families might adapt. The second concern is biological. Morning light is the main signal that keeps the body's internal clock, or circadian rhythm, aligned with the solar day. When that signal arrives later, the clock tends to drift later as well, which can disturb sleep, mood, and appetite. Teenagers, whose internal clocks already run late, may be especially vulnerable.

Supporters of permanent DST respond that these costs must be weighed against real benefits. Lighter evenings may encourage children and adults to exercise outdoors after school or work, and some argue that they could reduce evening traffic accidents and certain kinds of crime, which tend to rise after dark. Others emphasize that the twice-yearly switch is itself disruptive: the spring transition, which costs people an hour of sleep, has been associated with short-term increases in accidents and health problems. From this perspective, ending the clock change is worthwhile even if winter mornings become darker.

Critics of the bill, including many sleep scientists, agree that the switching should stop but argue that the country is choosing the wrong permanent setting. They favor permanent standard time, which keeps clocks closer to the position of the sun. One proposed compromise, delaying school start times so that students still travel in daylight, faces its own difficulty. As the University of Washington team points out, if every schedule simply moves an hour later, society has effectively returned to standard time while keeping the label of daylight saving. Later starts would also collide with parents' working hours and after-school activities.

The debate illustrates a broader lesson about public policy: a measure that seems to offer something for nothing usually redistributes costs rather than eliminating them. Brighter evenings are visible and pleasant, while darker mornings are experienced mostly by people with little political voice, such as children waiting at bus stops. Whether permanent DST is a sensible reform may therefore depend less on the total amount of daylight, which no law can change, than on whose hours of light a society decides to protect.

articles.title: Search, AI, and the Classroom: Who Should Decide?
articles.dek: Google now switches off AI for students by default, but Search goes with it. Is that a choice, or pressure?
paras: For years, students in many schools have logged into a Google Classroom account, typed a question into Google Search, and begun their homework. That routine may soon change. On November 3, 2026, Google announced that its artificial intelligence tools, including the Gemini chatbot and Gemini in Classroom, will be switched off by default for student accounts in primary and secondary schools, known in the United States as K-12. School administrators will have to turn them on explicitly. The surprise lay in what was tied to them: Google Search will also be unavailable to those accounts unless the school opts in to the AI tools. Critics quickly argued that the policy left schools with an uncomfortable choice.

The announcement is the latest turn in a year of rapid change. In August, Google made Gemini available to many K-12 students, having previously restricted it to users aged 18 and over, and the move provoked an outcry from parents and advocacy groups. Earlier, the nonprofit Common Sense Media had rated Google's AI-powered search an "unacceptable risk" for young users, reporting that it readily completed homework assignments and sometimes repeated misinformation with an air of authority. Google dismissed the testing as narrow, but the criticism added pressure. In its announcement, the company presented the new defaults as a response to such concerns: school leaders, it said, should control how AI is used in their classrooms.

Why, then, did the change provoke fresh objections? The key issue is the link between two products that schools may wish to treat separately. Many educators regard a search engine as basic infrastructure, as essential to research as a library catalogue, while they view chatbots with far more caution. Under the new arrangement, a district that wants students to keep using Google Search must also accept Google's AI tools. Lina Khan, the former chair of the US Federal Trade Commission, wrote that Google was "using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI." Josh Golin of the children's advocacy group Fairplay went further, urging schools to turn off Google's AI tools and consider more privacy-protective search engines.

Google's defenders can point to several counterarguments. First, the default is now "off," which gives schools a decision they did not have when Gemini was simply switched on. Second, Google argues that its tools are designed to support learning rather than replace it. The company is adding a feature called Guided Learning, which, when it detects certain homework requests, walks students through a topic step by step instead of supplying an answer immediately. Google says its own research shows measurable learning gains, and it describes the goal as "productive struggle": challenge that stretches students without overwhelming them. From this perspective, combining search and AI simply reflects how information is now found online.

Skeptics respond that research conducted by a company about its own product deserves careful scrutiny, and that the scale of Google's presence in education changes the nature of the choice. According to the company, about 150 million students and teachers worldwide use Google Classroom, and many schools depend on inexpensive Chromebook laptops built around Google's software. For such schools, abandoning Google Search is not a realistic option, so an "opt-in" may function, in practice, more like a requirement. Some large districts have chosen caution instead: New York City and Los Angeles have temporarily banned generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools while they develop policies.

The deeper question concerns who should decide how young people encounter new technology. Technology companies possess the engineering expertise and can update products quickly, but their commercial interest in building habits early is obvious. Schools know their students and curricula, yet many lack the time and technical staff to evaluate complex tools. Parents, meanwhile, are often consulted last. A defensible policy would probably separate basic access to information from optional AI features, allowing each school to judge them independently. Whether Google will offer that flexibility remains unclear; the company says it will share details with schools in the coming months, before the changes take effect.

articles.title: Counting the Uncounted: The True Scale of the Global Wildlife Trade
articles.dek: More than 107,000 species are bought and sold, most of them legally. Can we call the trade sustainable if no one is counting?
paras: When people hear the phrase "wildlife trade," they tend to picture smuggled ivory, tiger parts, or pangolin scales seized at an airport. Those images are accurate but incomplete. A study published in Science Advances by researchers at the University of Melbourne has found that at least 107,356 species of plants, animals, and fungi are used and traded around the world, more than twice the previous estimate of about 50,000. The finding suggests that the commerce in living things is far broader, and far less understood, than either the public or policymakers have assumed.

Much of this trade is both legal and familiar. It includes timber for furniture and construction, seafood, medicinal plants, cut flowers, mushrooms and other fungi, and animals and ornamental fish sold as pets. According to the study, the legal trade is worth roughly ten times as much as the illegal trade that dominates headlines. In other words, much of the pressure that trade places on wild species may come not from criminal networks but from ordinary consumer demand, satisfied through lawful supply chains that rarely attract attention.

Arriving at the new figure required combining records from wildlife trade monitoring programs, and the process exposed how patchy those records are. The researchers note that the United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of species groups. For most traded species, there is little or no information about how many individuals are taken, where they come from, or how wild populations are responding. "For most of these species we have little to no data," said the lead researcher, Professor Alice Hughes. As a result, the authors warn, the true number of traded species is probably even higher than their estimate.

This gap matters because trade is not inherently harmful. Many species can be harvested sustainably, and for millions of people, especially in rural communities, collecting and selling wild products is an important source of income. Sustainable use can even support conservation by giving local people a financial reason to protect forests and fisheries. The difficulty is that sustainability can only be demonstrated with evidence. Without population data, no one can tell whether a particular orchid, reef fish, or tree is being harvested at a rate it can withstand, or whether it is quietly being pushed toward collapse.

Current international policy addresses only a small part of the problem. The trade target in the global biodiversity framework, the agreement under which governments have pledged to halt the loss of nature, covers only about 2 to 3 percent of the species now known to be traded, leaving roughly 97 percent outside its scope. Hughes argues that this mismatch weakens efforts to protect nature and could undermine the framework's goals. "Without better data, we cannot accurately assess risks to biodiversity," she said.

The authors therefore call for a coordinated global monitoring system with standardized data collection, so that information gathered in different countries can be compared. Rather than building an entirely new bureaucracy, they suggest adapting processes that already exist, such as customs checks and the inspections that animals and animal products undergo to prevent the spread of disease. Opponents of stronger regulation might respond that additional reporting would burden small traders and poorer exporting countries, and that tracking more than 100,000 species is unrealistic. Supporters reply that the costs of ignorance are higher: a species that disappears cannot be restored by later paperwork.

The study ultimately reframes a familiar issue. Protecting wildlife is often presented as a contest between conservationists and poachers, but the larger challenge may be making everyday trade visible. Consumers who buy a houseplant, a fish fillet, or a wooden table rarely consider which species they are using or where it came from. Until governments can answer those questions systematically, the claim that the world's wildlife trade is sustainable will remain, at best, an untested assumption.

words.def: able to continue without causing long-term damage

words.def: the range of things that something deals with

keySentences.text: The finding suggests that the commerce in living things is far broader, and far less understood, than either the public or policymakers have assumed.
keySentences.note: The thesis: the trade is both bigger and less understood than people think. Main-idea and summary questions build on this.

keySentences.text: According to the study, the legal trade is worth roughly ten times as much as the illegal trade that dominates headlines.
keySentences.note: A surprising comparison that challenges the common image of wildlife trade. Watch how numbers are used in answer choices.

keySentences.text: For most traded species, there is little or no information about how many individuals are taken, where they come from, or how wild populations are responding.
keySentences.note: This lists exactly what data is missing. Negative factual questions often test lists like this.

keySentences.text: The difficulty is that sustainability can only be demonstrated with evidence.
keySentences.note: The turning point of paragraph 4: after admitting trade can be good, the author explains why data still matters.

keySentences.text: Supporters reply that the costs of ignorance are higher: a species that disappears cannot be restored by later paperwork.
keySentences.note: A response to the opposing view. Notice the concession-and-reply structure, which is useful in TOEFL writing.

keySentences.text: Until governments can answer those questions systematically, the claim that the world's wildlife trade is sustainable will remain, at best, an untested assumption.
keySentences.note: The conclusion. “At best” shows the author's cautious but critical attitude.
